reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When building models that make binary choices, we often need a way to turn any raw score—ranging from negative infinity to positive infinity—into a clean probability between zero and one. Linear functions fail here because they grow without bound. We need a curve that flattens out at both ends while providing a smooth transition in the middle.

Pierre François Verhulst faced a similar problem when modeling population growth constrained by limited resources. He used the logistic function, a classic sigmoid curve, to represent how growth decelerates as it approaches a carrying capacity. By scaling the input and shifting its midpoint, this function maps the entire real line onto a bounded interval.

At the heart of this behavior is the exponential term in the denominator. As inputs become very large and negative, the exponent grows large and positive, causing the denominator to explode and driving the output to zero. As inputs become very large and positive, the exponent goes to zero, leaving the fraction at one. The steepness parameter controls how rapidly this transition occurs around the midpoint.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic sigmoid maps any real input to a bounded output between zero and one. Adjust the steepness, midpoint, and marker to examine the curve and its slope.
